I shall not take up much time of the House in discussing the principles of the Bill as I have done that on a former occasion, nor shall I discuss at any length the motives of the provincial government in making the changes to the law which they did make. I shall point out the facts and I shall refer more particularly to the riding of Thunder Bay and Rainy River with which I am most familiar, but I believe the same conditions or nearly the same conditions obtain in a .majority of the ridings in the new section of Ontario. Mr. Speaker, on a former occasion in the House I said that the time allowed would not permit of the preparation of proper lists or for an appeal against the lists if the Ontario elections were to be held upon a certain day. When I spoke then I was not certain that the elections would be held on the 8th of June but that afterwards turned out to be the date and the statements I made on that occasion have been verified by the facts. The elections were held on the 8th of June and I again assert that the lists were illegal lists; that there really was no list and ho justification for the course adopted so far as that riding was concerned. I have the Act here but I shall not detain the House by reading the sections of it to which I refer, however, as to the provisions of the Act I have no less authority than the hon. member for Sault St. Marie (Mr. Boyce) who when he spoke on a former occasion in the House told us that the law provided that appeals may be taken to a county court judge and that the county court judge could not fix less than 30 days after the enumerator had posted his list for the hearing of the appeal under the statute of 1907. My hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) argued very strongly and at great length that 30 days was short enough, and I agreed with him then and I agree with him now. The facts are that after the list is posted up by the enumerator you have to find out whether he has included the names of those who are entitled to be put on the list, and in a new country like northern Ontario it practically means another revision of the lists, for you have to go over the same ground the enumerator has gone over, and if you do not, then when the election comes on you will find that a large number of names that should have been on the list are omitted and that a large number are on the list that should not be there at all. Now I could take up a good deal of time in showing that the lists recently prepared have on them a large number of names who are not entitled to be on. I make this statement, that names are put on in one riding, a large number of

whom reside in another riding. That may have been an error, I do not say it was deliberately done.
Where was the polling place?

Kaministiquia. They were in Fort William division, not in the Port Arthur division. Their place of residence was in the other riding altogether. The Kamanistiquia poll is in the riding of Port Arthur, and perhaps seventy-five of them altogether was put on the list.
I am not contending that that was done purposely, but I have heard men say that it was. But I think I am correct in stating that a considerable number of them voted, and notwithstanding that some of them were challenged they voted. I know of another case where, if my information is correct, a large number of men were put on the list in the mine centre or that vicinity. They were only a few days in the country and they were not Canadians at all. The scrutineer on the other side cautioned them that they were subject to punishment; he swore a lot of them, and over 40 of them voted notwithstanding that they knew they were not entitled to vote. Certain other parties said ; Poll your vote, and we will see you through.
Was this in a Dominion election?
In the last provincial election. But the same conditions might arise if he were compelled to go to vote upon that list.
Does not the hon. gentleman know that that sort of thing happens all over Canada? There will be accidents under every regime.

To a certain extent there may be, but it is a very unusual thing for men to be put on a voters' list in one riding who reside in another riding. I am only showing that the list is defective. I could give many more reasons. Now, I state that there has been no appeal. Why? In the first place the law of 1907 provides that a list shall be made biennially. There was a two years' suspension of that, which expired some time in February last. Under that law the provincial officials were bound to make a list. The dutv of the enumerators is to prepare a list commencing not later than the 1st of July in each year. They could not do that in this case because the list had been suspended for two years, but they were bound to commence after that time had expired. Why didn't they commence the list? I can only say that they did not commence the list because they were not instructed. The blame may lie on the government themselves. But certainly they did not commence the list in February ; they commenced it in March. They commenced under the law of
1907, which provides for 30 days after the enumerator has posted his list.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: By what authority does the hon. gentleman say they were commenced in March?
Of my own knowledge.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is he speaking of the six ridings?

I am speaking of the riding of Thunder Bay and Rainy River.
I know of my own knowledge that the enumerators were out in March.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does he say that before March there were no enumerators at work in that riding?
I do not say that there were none before that, but that came to my knowledge some time in March.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What then is the hon. gentleman's point?

My point is this, that the enumerators proceeded under the law of 1907 until the list was about half prepared, in several divisions of that riding, then the law of 1908 comes in and cuts that law out. Instead of thirty days it is cut down to fifteen so far as the enumerators are concerned. The time to appeal to a judge instead of being thirty days, will only be ten days.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken, it is 15 days.
I am not mistaken, I have the Act in my hand. It is 15 days after the enumerator has posted his list.
The hon. gentleman' said 10 days.

I did not say 10 days, the hon. gentleman was not listening to my argument. I say there are 15 days for the appeal after the enumerator has posted his list; if you appeal to the judge he may fix only ten. I have the Act here, fifteen days are given after the list is'posted up by the enumerator. Now, there is where an injustice has taken place. After the lists have been prepared on the basis of 60 days, the 60 are cut down to 20 days. Those who knew the law of 1907 would have had time to put in their appeal if the list had been prepared according to the law upon which they were proceeding at first. But a new law comes in and cuts that out, and then they had fewer days to act. There is this further objection after that law did come into effect. I want to ask any hon. gentleman opposite if he thinks the average elector, one in fifty of the electors of that riding, knew anything about the law of 1908 when it first came into force. Let me say this to the House, the law was not an amendment to the Election Act, if it had been, it might have come to the knowledge of some electors. But that was not the case. These two provisions I have

referred to were embodied in the Statute Law Amendment Bill as I understand it as an afterthought placed in the Statute Law Amendment Act. Now, I know for a fact that no elector could, on the day of the election, on the 8th of June, secure the Act.
The kon. gentleman is not correct; that is not in the Act.

My kon. friend does not know the Act. If he will look at it he will find the sections referred to are not in the Election Act. They are in the Statute Law Amendment Act now as reprinted, the sections are in the Voters' List Act.
They were put in the Consolidated Act.

My hon. friend can call it the Consolidated Act if he pleases, but it is the Act that is passed every year at the end of the session, as the Statute Law Amendment Act, and no elector thinks of going to find an amendment to the Voters' Act there. In my riding there was not a lawyer on the day of the election who knew anything about it. The average elector could not get advice ; he could not find the law ; it was not in existence, it was not where he could lay his hand on it. The lawyers throughout my riding, I went to several of them myself, and not one of them knew anything about it.
Does my hon. friend say that he did not know it at the time ?
I did not know it except from the newspaper reports.
I have my hon. friend's speech delivered on the 6th May in which he refers to criticism of the amendment.
I did. I referred to that, but it was only as a rumour. Did my hon. friend have a copy of the law on the 8th June?
I do not know that I had.
I do not think the hon. gentleman had. If he had he was favoured. We could not get it. I will go farther and say there was not even fair dealing in that.
Does my hon. friend not say that the notice of this amendment was published before the 6th May in the Port Arthur newspaper to which he referred in the House on the 6th of May ?

Certainly. I say so now but it was nothing but newspaper report. Does my hon. friend take the law from the newspapers ? Does he expect voters to go and enter an appeal upon an article published in a newspaper ?

There was sufficient law to justify my hon. friend as a member of the House in prophesying that no election would be held in any of the new ridings in Mr. CONMEE.
Ontario because of the change in the law and the irregularities of the list.
Quite correct; there was enough iu the newspaper report to justify that argument, but there was not enough to enable any elector to take an appeal against the voters' list.

My hon. friend, after reading the account of the amendment which was published in the Port Arthur ' Chronicle,' said that he believed the statement was substantially correct and he went on to argue upon that proposition that the elections could not be held by reason of the shortness of time.

It is probable that that is correct, but would that justify an elector-in entering an appeal or did that provide the machinery for an appeal ? I am not discussing the question. I say it was a matter of newspaper report.
Surely, if it justifies one thing it justifies another.

No, it does not. Not only was the right of the electors taken away by the new law which cut the time down from sixty days to twenty, but there was no law, no machinery provided or any means placed at the disposal of the electors or even at the disposal of the legal advisers of the people by which they could avail themselves of the law in that respect.
At one o'clock, House took recess.
House resumed at three o'clock.

At one o'clock I was speaking of the voters' list in the province of Ontario in the territory without municipal organization. 1 had pointed out that the list as prepared was not a fair list and that to secure a fair list other machinery would be necessary. I had pointed out very grave defects in the manner in which the lists were prepared in these particular cases. In the first instance the Ontario law provides that there shall be a notice or proclamation with regard to the preparation of the lists, and I am informed and believe that no such proclamation was issued and that no notice of any kind was given to the public. I know for a fact that the enumerators had been preparing the lists for some sections for 'three or four weeks before any of the Liberals in the locality were aware the work was going on. Another objection was that all the enumerators were extreme partisans nominated by the prospective Conservative candidates, and were I to use the language of gentlemen on the other side in regard to that I might describe it as a very grave wrong. Another objection is that in some instances the enumerators posted the lists in an outside riding fifty or more miles from the place of residence of the electorate

interested, and I have evidence here of that very grave wrong-doing. The law provides that the lists shall be prepared as nearly as may he under the same rules, regulations, and procedure, so far as practicable as the list is prepared in the municipality, and the clerk of the municipality is required to posit up his list, and the voter has thirty days within which to examine the list and appeal. Would it not be absurd if a municipal clerk were to go to another municipality fifty miles away to post his list and claim he bad given proper notice. I have the list here which was prepared for the Silver Mountain division and there is a notice on it which says : This list was posted up in the enumerator's office at Port Arthur on the 5th day of June, 1908. Silver Mountain is in the Fort William riding more than fifty miles from Port Arthur, and it is extraordinary to conceive how the voters could take advantage of their right to appeal within fifteen days under such notice. So far as I know this list may have been sent to the locality but I am not aware of it. I have been told by some of the electors they never knew there was such a list until the fifteen days had elapsed, but how that may be I am not prepared to say.
Does the hon. gentleman say that a copy of that list was not posted in the polling subdivision ?
X have just explained that I was not saying so as a matter of my own knowledge.
The hon. gentleman does not say the list was not posted in the proper place ?

I say there is no evidence so far as I know of its having been posted. It might have been posted but that has nothing to do with my argument, and after I had made that statement it was unnecessary for the hon. gentleman to ask the question. Some hon. gentlemen stated in the House to-day that it was not true that the list had not run the full time for appeals previous to the day of polling, but this list here is proof, because it says it was posted in the enumerator's office on the 5th of June and the election took place on the 8th of June. Therefore there can be no doubt that in that particular case-and I have other similar cases here-there was not time to appeal and the list was absolutely void as a proper list on which to hold the election. If hon. gentlemen opposite have the curiosity to see these lists I shall be glad to send them over. Another objection is that the enumerators started to prepare the lists under the law of 1907, and that the law of 1908 came into operation before the list was completed. And in view of the fact that the time for appeal was reduced under the amended law the electorate were deprived of rights which should have
been preserved to them. They were taken by surprise and as a result a proper list could not be prepared. But a more serious objection still is in the fact that the law of 1907 provided thirty days for appeals after the list was posted up by the enumerator. The law was that when the list had been posted up for the time required and the lists printed, then that was the list against which an appeal could be taken. In this instance I think the law has not been changed in that regard. The procedure has been changed, and, I am informed, by instructions from the government at Toronto, those instructions being that each polling subdivision should be dealt with by itself, and that the fifteen days should run from the posting up of the list of each particular subdivision, and that unless it was appealed against within the fifteen days, the list of that polling subdivision became a legal list, and appeals from it were refused afterwards. That is, I believe, the view held by the enumerators who prepared the list. Under the list as prepared and posted previous to the coming into effect of the law of 1908, even if that law had reached the knowledge of the electors, as it did not until long afterwards, the fifteen days in some cases had elapsed, and there could not be any appeal. Sui ely it will be admitted that that was not fair. That involves, in the riding to which I refer, perhaps fifty per cent of the people. I do not think I need take up the time of the House to go over the sections to show that that is not what was contemplated by the Act. The list to be appealed against is the entire list. That has always been the practice. The list was never prepared before in the manner which I have described; nobody ever heard of it; nobody was prepared for such a procedure, and therefore everybody was taken by surprise and at a disadvantage. The statute says that the list shall be the whole list. The appeal is to lie, not against each subdivision of the list; that would involve fifty appeals in the case to which I have referred. It is quite clear, under the form of notice given by the judge under the Act of 1908, that it was one list, and not forty or fifty divisions of the list, that was contemplated by the statute. This notice, form 24, is in these words:
Take notice that the undersigned will be in attendance at	at the hour of
on the day of	to hear appeals with
respect to the voters' list for the electoral district of	.
I do not think it could be properly contended that fifty divisions of a list could possibly have been in the minds of the framers of this Act, for all the other forms are to the same effect, while there are a large number of sections of the Act which sfiow clearly that it is a complete list that is referred to. It is beyond dispute that the procedure in the municipal!-

ties show that it is the entire list against which an appeal may be taken, and not a subdivision of a list. If that is so, the statute has been violated in nearly every case. Another objection, which I think is of importance as sufficient to show that this list has been ill-prepared, and that the people have been deprived of their rights under it, lies in the fact to which I have already referred, that the list was posted on the 5tli day of .Tune. That shows that there could not be any appeal against it. Now, I want to meet any objection that might be raised to that part of my argument. For instance, it might be claimed that I or any elector might take an appeal. I do not know that it would be open to me to take an appeal, because by referring to form 5 of the Act it will be seeu how difficult is to take these appeals. The procedure is there set out pretty elaborately. The party taking the appeal, I assume, must be an elector in the division or in the unorganized territory. An elector in an organized municipality would have a right to take an appeal in that municipality. I do not suppose he would have a right to take an appeal in an unorganized territory of which he was not an elector. Therefore to get an appeal you have to go out to the district where the electors reside, which in some cases is a long distance-from 100 to 150 or even 200 miles from the centre where the appeal would be lodged with the judge who might be called upon to act. Then I point out that as to the portions of the list already prepared, the new law cut in and took away the right to appeal which formerly existed because the time had elapsed or was about to elapse. Then, as to the list to be prepared after that law came into force. I still point out that even if the electors had a knowledge of the fact-not a newspaper report; I do not think it can be contended that a reference in a newspaper constitutes a legal or proper law that can be taken notice of in the way of an appeal; even if they had the notice, under tl\e machinery necessary to put the law in motion, the time is entirely inadequate and unfair. The whole argument of my hon. friend from Sanlt Ste. Marie, in his recent speech, found fault with the time, which in one instance I think was four! days shorter; but the difference as between six days and ten days would not be very great. Now, you have to go and And the elector; you have to give his name and age and all the other particulars about him; you have to find upon what list he is, what are the grounds of his being entitled to be upon the list; and, on the other hand, you have to find what are the names and post office addresses of othej parties whose names are on the list, and on what grounds you propose to exclude them from the list. All this is to be filed with the judge previous to the time of the appeal, and within the fifteen days allowed.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman upon wjiat clause of the Act he bases his assertion that the appellant must live in the unorganized territory?

On form 5 and on the general terms of the Act; and I am quite sure that I am right, because a case has been decided in the courts on this point ip which the courts held that the appellant must be a resident of the polling division in which he is making the appeal.
Under this new Act?

Oh, no, this Act is not yet in force. The sections of the Act to which I am referring are in the Act of 1907. The new sections would have nothing to do with the procedure in an appeal. They have only shortened the time. They have made some changes in the procedure in preparing the lists, but no changes, so far as I know, in the action of the court in dealing with the case after the court becomes seized of it. If the hon- gentleman will take the trouble to read the form given for the appeal he will see that all I have stated is quite borne out. I submit that that procedure cannot be satisfactorily carried out under the provisions of the Act as it stands.
But I wish to go a step further. Suppose we throw away that contention about this particular list, I think I have given facts enough to show that this list was prepared in violation of the rights of the electors, and never should have been forced on the electors in any section of the country. But to drop that part of the argument, what position would we be in if we did not pass this or some other Bill of this nature? If our election comes on when the lists are more than a year old, we are restricted to the machinery of the present law which experience proves to have operated badly. I think the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce)-though I by no means agree in everything he said-was warranted in making a strong complaint reg rdiug the operation of the present law. Does the hon. gentleman want that sort of thing repeated? If he does not, will he point out how, under the present Act, it can be avoided? But suppose an election comes on when the lists are not more than a year old, do hon. gentlemen think it fair that the election should be held on lists prepared under the conditions I have pointed out?

I deny emphatically that there was anything wrong with the lists in the riding I represent.
Mr. CONMEE My hon. friend represents a pretty old riding and has not more than a township or two which would come under the new clause. If he has any unorganized territory, it is very small and but few electors are affected. But in my riding the Act affects thousands of electors and also in Nipissing. I submit that it would be un-

fair to force these lists in such ridings upon
the electorate in any election. Then if we ignore the demand altogether and decide that the election shall be held on these lists -these stuffed lists against which there could be no appeal ; lists which were not municipal lists, but made by partisans in violation of section after section of the Act-we shall be deliberately preventing the will of the people from making itself felt. There is nothing in the provincial machinery to remedy this because the Act of 1908 takes away the former right enjoyed by the electorate. It cuts the time down to fifteen and ten days and you cannot in that time have a fair list, I do not care who prepares it. The provincial authorities have the right, notwithstanding they have a list, should the Dominion elections go on to-morrow, to order a new list. They might appoint strong partisans and prepare a list in violation of the rights and liberties of the people, under the Franchise Act, as they did before. I do not want to be understood as holding the opinion that they would. I do not hold it altogether. I think that some of the errors may have been unintentional but others were intentional. I am not called on to go into the reasons for this inequality and wrong in the preparation of the lists. But on the 8th June the Liberals were forced to accept these stuffed lists or take an appeal. But in the latter case, the Liberal candidates would only have been thrown over to a by-election, which would have been equally unfair. No man ought to be placed in that position by the action of any government.
Would that be any more unfair iu Ontario than in Quebec ?

I think that is unfair anywhere. If there is a reasonable opportunity to hold the elections on the same day, it would not be fair to hold them on different days, no matter in what province that might be done.
The hon. gentleman complains about the want of time, what would he suggest as the time necessary to properly compile the lists in new Ontario ?

In my opinion I would give thirty days to the entire list-not the divisions of the list against which I have been complaining. After the enumerator in the unorganized sections had prepared his list and printed and distributed it, then thirty days should run for an appeal. After those thirty days there should be thirty days for the judge to hold his court.
How much for your primary appeal from the enumerators ?
Thirty days.
Two periods of thirty days each.	i
That would be my idea.
Then there would be the additional time used in printing and the time required by the judge to insert his advertisement.

After the enumerator posts up his list and allows his time, he should have the list printed and prepared for distribution. That has always been done with regard to the new lists. The hon. member shakes his head.
I think I know just as much about it as the hon. gentleman.
Perhaps in the hon. gentleman's district. Then I would say the enumerators in his district are not quite as up to date as they are elsewhere.
The enumerators in Algoma are as correct and up to date as any in Canada.

I have to take my hon. friend's word for that because I know nothing to the contrary, but it is not quite courteous for the hon. gentleman to impugn my statement because I know that has been the practice. The sheriffs were the enumerators. In my riding for the last couple of elections while I was in provincial politics, Sheriff Thompson was the enumerator, and I know he had his lists all ready as soon as the time was up and he would not give any one a list before.
Do you mean he had the list printed when the last court was held ?
I did not say when the last court was held.

When would he get
them printed ?

He could have them all set up in the printer's office and have them struck off as soon as the time for an appeal had expired. He does not need to wait until his last court is held to have the list printed.
Out of wffiich 30 days would he take that time ?

My hon. friend is arguing against himself. In this last preparation of the lists directions came from the Attorney General at Toronto not only to regard each polling subdivision as a list but saying that after the fifteen days ran, they should have them printed and have the judge sign them, which they did. That did not make them any more legal because they were in violation of other sections of the statute.
The point I am making is that under the Ontario Act of 1908, you cannot have a fair list in an unorganized territory, whatever it may be in one or two ridings ; you cannot have it in Nipissing or Sault Ste. Marie or Rainy River, because the time is not afforded to have it. You might send an

army of men but I submit you cannot have an intelligent and proper appeal to protect the rights either of the electorate or of a political party under the provisions of the statute as it stands to-day. The condition of that list is certainly such as to call for a strong protest from every - man of any political faith.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have contended that they want only a fair list. We proclaim that we want only a fair list. If that is true why not take the opportunity to make a fair list ? An offer has been made in this Bill to have the judges prepare the lists, appoint the enumerators and conduct the machinery, revise the list and hand it out in a fair manner. If hon. gentlemen are not willing to accept that, where does it place them ? It places them in the position that having obtained the list by misrepresentation-I shall not use a stronger word- by a violation of the statute and the natural rights of the electors that gives them an advantage, they want to force that list upon their opponents, irrespective of either law or natural justice. The hon. member said that you can appeal against the lists ; and if they are contrary to law you can have them made right. Who will put them right and how long will it take ? Who will put up the money to fight a contest against the provincial government ? I submit it is not a fair proposition. The fair thing to do is here, to-day, to take this Act and if it is not what I think it is, a fair Act, to make it a fair Act and put it in force in order that when the elections come on we will go with confidence to the poll, believing that every man who was entitled to a vote is on the list and that no man has been struck off the list because of his party or other reasons to give an advantage to any candidate. That is the kind of list we want and if hon. gentlemen are not willing to accept it they must assume the responsibility for rejecting it.
To what other polling subdivisions, if any, besides Kaministiquia would you refer to specifically as being open to objection in regard to the making up of the lists ?

Since my hon. friend puts his question in that way, every polling division in my riding. There is not a legal list or a proper list, I say it is a stuffed list in every polling division, but I do not say that tie same conditions exist in all divisions as at Kaministiquia and some other places.

I had not intended and did not think it was necessary for me to offer any remarks upon the ' amendment before the House, on the second reading of this Bill. The debate on the second reading was adjourned by my hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) on the 18th day of May and here Mr. ( UNMEE.
on the 2nd day of July, after what we believe to be a period of negotiations, we come down to the second reading of this Bill. The Prime Minister allows the hon. member for South Grey to resume the debate on the second reading of the Bill without offering any comments, without giving the House any information whatever as to the reason of the delay that has taken place, to which the government has been a party and of which it has been the cause. He allows the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River, to resume the debate on this amendment and to discuss every particular of the Bill itself, not confining himself to the amendment although he had spoken once upon the Bill, and explaining why the section as originally introduced should be passed and why there should be necessity for a remedy although the hon. gentleman had at very great length given the very same arguments before in speaking of this Bill.

I did not make any representations that the Bill should be passed in its original form either when I spoke last or this time. In my previous speech I pointed out some sections in the Bill which required amendment. The hon. gentleman is not justified in quoting me as he has done.

What I mean to say is this, that for over a month past my hon. friend has been circulating throughout this country literature and rumours to the effect that the opposition has been obstructing the business of this House. He keeps silent while he professes to be negotiating, according to a statement he made upon the second reading of the Bill, to amend the clauses of this Bill in a manner which will suit the interests of the majority of the members of this House. And when the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) has completed his address, an address of two hours, the right hon. gentleman leading the House sits silent while the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) expatiates, not upon the amendment-not one word about Manitoba to which only the amendment refers-but he expatiates on the iniquities committed in making up these lists which have called for some interference on the part of this parliament. I did not expect it would be necessary to say anything at all upon the second reading of this Bill. But it does seem to me that it ill becomes the right hon. gentleman to complain that the opposition has been obstructing the business of the House while he himself demonstrates, on the resumption of the second reading, that he is in exactly the same position as he was on the 18th of May.
Now, a word with regard to what has been said by the hon. member for 'South

Grey (Mr. Miller) and the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. ICon-mee). We are always pleased on this side of the House to listen to advice, especially when it comes from so eminent a quarter as the hon. member for South Grey with regard to the legislation that is adapted for the unorganized districts. The hon. member for Rainy River asks us what remedy there is in case a provincial list is more than one year old, what remedy there is if this Bill does not become law? There was a remedy, as my hon. friend knows right well, in 1904, and it is a little late for my hon. friend, after being elected by a majority of 500 or 600 in those same bush polls made up of illegal lists, to come down to this House now and say: Those lists made up in the unorganized territories, by which I profited, were irregular and improper lists, and I think any one is justified in raising objection to them. Did any one hear any objection from the hon. member for Thunder Bay until now when he wants something better?

The hon. member is mistaken about any such lists being prepared in the riding of Thunder Bay. There was ample time for an appeal. As a matter of fact, if he will go to the Secretary of State's office he will find that Judge Fitzgerald sat 21 days hearing appeals. Nobody complained of the lists after they were finished.

As a political juggler the hon. gentleman cannot be surpassed. When he made his speech on the 6th day of May he absolutely denied that any such lists were made up in his riding. I will read what he said on page 8229:
Does the hon. member say that the lists were not made up in his riding under the law at the last election?
Yes, I have made that statement.
I am very much surprised to hear it.

I was the candidate, and I have no knowledge of any lists being made under Dominion officials.
The next day the hon. gentleman rises in his place and is compelled by his line of argument to say : Yes, yesterday I was mistaken, there were lists made up in my riding under the orders in council which have heen complained of. Yet those are the lists which my hon. friend now says were improper and improvident, and which I was justified in complaining about. There was only one order in council providing for the preparation of lists in all those northern Ontario ridings, and if they were bad in West Algoma they were bad and unjustifiable in Thunder Bay. My hon. friend can recollect the facts when he finds it convenient to do so. He will find there was one order in council dated the 25th of August, 1904, the one under which all the 372
voters' lists were made up, and under the authority of which all the enumerators were appointed, and some of them in Thunder Bay and Rainy River, I have no doubt, pursued the usual practice.

I wish to correct the hon. member. In pointing out that the lists were prepared under provincial machinery, I am not arguing with him as to whether there were one or more orders in council. That does not touch the point at all. The order in council was acted upon in the riding I refer to early enough to give ample time. There was no complaint upon that score. The order was not acted upon in his riding, according to his statement. I do not complain of the lists in my riding, I only referred to the complaint of my hon. friend. I take him as an authority. If he wishes to destroy his own argument I have no objection.
Then my hon. friend says there were no such lists made up in his riding, although he contradicted that assertion the next day.
No, my honoured friend quotes me wrong again.
The hon. gentleman asserts, and contradicts, and asserts again so often that I cannot make out what he means.

I would rather make the assertions myself than to allow my honoured friend to make them. I stated to him that there was no appeal. He has quoted me wrongly. I stated there was no appeal in my riding. I was mistaken in that. I found upon examination of the records in the office of the iSecretary of State that there was an appeal, that in one of the Thunder Bay divisions there was an appeal, the judge sat 21 days hearing an appeal. In the Rainy River division there was no appeal. That is what I had in my mind at the time I spoke.

My hon. friend is not satisfied with the law as it exists. My hon. friend was satisfied in 1904 with the law as it then existed, although in 1904, as he knows perfectly well, no provincial lists had been made up since prior to 1902 and there was no list there that was not one, yes, two years old. The law then was good enough for my hon. friend. The lists were made up under that law and that law is on the statute book to-day. My hon. friend says : What are you going to do if there is not a provincial list in force which is not over a year old ? What I have to say is that I do not retract one of the complaints I have made in the House in the last few years in which I was so abundantly justified and I am glad of the hon. gentleman(s endorsation in that respect. Take that law as it is, apply it to the conditions as they



are found to exist, namely, give time for the making up of the lists under Dominion authority, make your time for appeal sufficient, make your time for enumeration sufficient and then you will have a condition of things that will meet any contingency which may occur from time to time instead of fastening upon a portion of the province of Ontario, as the right hon. gentleman proposes to do, a law for all time that is an unjust and unfair discrimination against that part of the province. I tell him, as I tell this House, that not only that portion of Ontario but every portion of Ontario will resent and resent very strongly indeed the action of the right hon. gentleman in this respect. It was a very extraordinary circumstance, Sir, that prior to that little event that happened on June 8 it was whispered around that the right hon. gentleman was not very keen about that part of the Bill which dealt with the northern part of Ontario. It was said that the increase in the representation of the provincial legislature of Ontario would give a great many seats to members in his own party in that part of Ontario and great events were looked for. The result of the election on June 8 was that there were eleven contests held in northern Ontario and eleven supporters of the Whitney government were elected with a Conservative plurality of about 4,000. Since then the right hon. gentleman has been very keen to have the law fastened on northern Ontario to punish the good people of those constituencies for having been so audacious as to express their opinion in favour of the good government of the Hon. J. P. Whitney. The people of Northern Ontario and of Canada will resent that discrimination and resent it very much. I would invite the right hon. gentleman to mature consideration of this step before he goes on with it. If he is to fasten these lists upon northern Ontario he must assume the responsibility for doing it and I desire, as a representative of northern Ontario, to protest most strongly against such a proceeding.

When the hon. gentleman speaks of discrimination what does he think the people of Canada will think of the discrimination of the Whitney government which gave thirty days for appeal in the organized parts of Ontario and cut It down to fifteen days in the unorganized parts ?

If my hon. friend will pardon me for answering an obscure question in this way I would say very shortly that the hon. gentleman's question was answered on the 8th day of June, 1908. Sections 7, 8 and 9 of the law as it exists to-day provide that the voters' lists in any unorganized district are not prepared at regular intervals but at such times as may be fixed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council or by order in Council. This government may appoint enumerators and may do ail the necessary acts in conformity with the law of the pro-Mr. BOYCE.
vince of Ontario under which the voters' lists are supposed to be made up and may carry out to completion, by the appointment of its own officers, the machinery of the provincial law. It is not the principle of that enactment that I have complained about but it is the manner in which it has been carried out. What I complained about was that while the statute requires that the provincial law shall and must be obeyed, it was not obeyed, carried out or conformed to in one particular. Therefore I say that if the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) had desired to be just and reasonable in this matter, if he had looked at the enactment as it was and as it appears, an enactment which will meet, for the time being, any contingency that exists, he would have offered to this House a very useful suggestion. But, as I said before, as long as he was a member of the Ontario House, as long as his friends there were making up the lists in the unorganized territories, as long as the sheriffs were appointed upon his nomination or by reason of his influence and as long as the deputies were appointed by the sheriffs upon his nomination, there were no better lists, nobody thought of complaining and if any one nad ever had the audacity in the legislature to complain about irregularities no voice would have been louder and no wrath would have appeared more righteous than those of the hon. gentleman. But, a change has come over the spirit of my hon. friend's dream. He suffered from a nightmare on June 25, 1905, when the whole control ot the lists was changed. No one can change quicker in his ideas than the hon. member and just as soon as the government changed my hon. friends ideas of the proper method of making out the voters' lists changed also. Although the legislative authority of Ontario was, in the time past and before that important date, a very excellent authority to make up these lists, in fact, the only authority which should make up these lists in any part of the country, now he says that the result of the working out of the same statute under a different government is fatal to the best interests of the people. How careful he is to conserve the lights of the people ! How jealous he is of the people's interests being trampled upon ! IIow careful he is to preserve them from any interruption or interference ! Is there an hon. gentleman in this House who has ever heard a cry from the northern districts that the lists were irregular except the roar of the non. member for Thunder Bay ? In so far as I have learned, and I have made careful inquiry with regard to the lists, far more careful inquiry than possibly my hon. friend will give me credit for, there is not one single complaint about the making up or revision of these lists, nor has it been charged that the manner of preparing these

lists lias affected the validity of one vote cast at that election. So much for my hon. friend. But, he was not long in ignorance in regard to how these lists were made up. My hon. friend conserves greatly the interests of that part of the riding. There was a gentleman to be elected mayor of Port Arthur, my hon. friend went up there, stayed there, appealed to the people and was on the hustings in order to secure the election of one of his own political complexion. The result was that my hon. friend's efforts were not as availing as they might have been because by the largest majority Port Arthur ever gave a gentleman who now occupies a seat in the legislative assembly in Ontario was elected mayor of Port Arthur Again Mr. Carriclr was the candidate in the provincial election, and my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) left this House to go there and try and defeat Mr. Garrick on these very lists, but once more Mr. Carrick was successful. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) went on the platform and he told them the same story as he tells us, but he told it with more license, because he was not on his responsibility as a member of the House of Commons. He told the people of Port Arthur that these lists were made up in the back office of Mr. Garrick's building, that they were made up by his partner, that they were absolutely spurious,, that nobody had the right to appeal, that they did not represent the voters in the constituency and, with his thunderous persuasive eloquence, he called upon the people to vote the government out of power that would consent to such fearful malpractice. The answer of the people was that they elected Mr. Carrick with a majority of several hundred. After the manner in which the people of his constituency have turned him down, it is little wonder that he comes back to this House and tries to hold up the public business by insisting that if the provisions of clause 1 of this Act are to be applied to any part of the Dominion they must apply -to the constituency he represents or else, as he says : Where am I? He has had two warnings, and he knows what the third will be. He is nervous and suffering, and therefore he comes before us to tell us a lot of stories about irregularities in the making up of the lists. The hon. member for South Grey could answer ime that he heard some one else say there were Irregularities, but I am afraid it was the member for Rainy River who whispered in his ear. And when I cornered the member for Rainy River by asking him to name one polling sub-division other than the Kaministiquia, he answered, with a wave of his hand : Oh, they are all wrong. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) knows it is dangerous to be specific, and hence he evaded the question I put to him. On May, the 6th, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee), speaking in this House, said (' Hansard,' page 8233) :
372$
Some time ago I gave my^ opinion to certain members of the provincial legislature that there was no intention on the part of the Ontario government to hold the elections in the new ridings on the same date as they would be held throughout the province. Mr. Whitney was cornered by the leader of the opposition and he made the statement that the elections would be held on the same date*
Now, listen to this prophet:
I ask hon. gentlemen to take note, I give my opinion for what it is worth, that the election will not be held in the new ridings on that day, Mr. Whitney to the contrary notwithstanding.
Read more of it.

I shall :
They will discover that irregularities exist, that the lists are not proper, and will find ways and means of holding these elections after the day fixed for the general elections.
If the hon. gentleman reads he will find my further statement that they would either have to postpone the election or hold it on lists without an appeal.
I will read till the hon. gentleman thinks he has had enough and tells me to stop.
Go right on, and if you do not get light you are quite dense.

I continue to quote from the remarks of my hon. friend :
I have it from very good authority, from a gentleman I believe to be in the confidence of the Conservative party that such is the intention, and I leave hon. gentlemen opposite to deal with their own friends in regard to that matter.
It would be a great feather in his cap if Mr. Whitney's word, given in the legislative assembly, should be disregarded and the elections postponed ; the hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) would have desired nothing better. But notwithstanding his prophecy, the elections in all the eleven constituencies of New Ontario were held on the 8th day of June, a day that my hon. friend will not soon forget. Now, in order that Mr. Whitney's word might be kept, there was in Kaministiquia a list containing 78 names which was not completed.
That list was completed.

The election was to be held on Monday and an appeal against the list was tiled with the enumerator on the Friday night preceding. That list containing 78 names was the only list that was known to be irregular, and the government was face to face with the question whether they should proceed with the election and allow as many of these 78 to vote as could take the oath, or whether there should be a breach of the understanding on account of this unavoidable circumstance and the elec-

tion postponed. Now, which was the better course? The validity of that list was not affected one bit by the holding of that election, and nobody knows it as well as my hon. friend.

The hon. gentleman is mistaken about the appeal. There was simply a letter written to the returning officer telling him that he was subject to a penalty if he allowed these people to vote. The time had run for that list, but I have five or six lists in my desk-
Give me the names.
1 cannot remember them all, but there are quite a number of lists for which the time had not run-Whitefish. North Lake, Conmee township.

There were 78 names on the Kaministiquia list, and had it not been for the appeal (and there was an appeal) that list would be certified on the following day. It was not certified on the following day, and feeling that less injustice would be done, the election was held upon that list. And let me tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) that members of his own party who were engaged in supporting the Liberal candidate were consulted with regard to that step, and they concurred in it and approved of it.
I never heard of anything of that kind.
The hon. gentleman differs from his party and from every one else when his own seat is affected.
The hon. gentleman is misinformed about that.

No, I am not. I have made very careful inquiry, and I am not speaking at random. The hon. gentleman cannot say how the voting on an uncompleted list in a provincial election in Kaministiquia could affect the validity of that list for the purpose of a Dominion election. Everybody knew what the procedure was for appeal, because there were appeals put in, and notwithstanding the holding of a provincial election, those appeals were dealt with.
There has been no appeal dealt with in the Thunder Bay district. My hon. friend is absolutely wrong.

With the utmost deference to my hon. friend, and knowing that he is never mistaken in any statement he makes, either in this House or out of it, I yvill ask him what court sat at Port Arthur on the 29th of May?
There was no appeal against the entire list What object is there in holding an appeal after the election is over?
What election?
The provincial election.

But it is the Dominion election which is to be affected by that appeal. If the provincial (election was held before the time for appeal had expired, surely the only argument was that the list for the purpose of that election was improper. The list was dealt with just the same as if that election had never been held. Appeal dates were appointed, and if there were no appeals against the list it was because there was nobody to appeal. Surely my hon. friend is not going to draw from the fact that nobody appealed the inference that anybody was deprived of his right to appeal. The fact of the election having taken place did not prevent the fifteen days running on. My hon. friend knows that the list has been certified all through that riding-examined by the judges, examined on appeal, and finally certified-and that to-day under the Ontario law a complete list stands there.
I know the contrary. I know that the list never has been revised. There has been no appeal against the list that has been disposed of.
I have seen the certificate of the judge and the letter of the judge to that effect.

I say there has been no appeal against the list. The only appeal that was ever taken was an appeal taken at my instance in those five or six divisions that I have been speaking about. What has become of them I do not know. I want to answer my hon. friend if he will allow me. He asks why appeals were not taken to protect the Dominion list? I answer that the appeals would have been taken but that the candidates in the 1 ical election took the position that such action would only play into the hinds of the Conservative candidates and throw the election over a by-election contest.

Now the House is let into the true secret that where the peoples' interests were concerned and where an appeal might have been taken for the advantage of the people, my hon. friend preferred to have a grievance rather than the remedy for the people-a grievance which he could bring down to this House and cast at the feet of the right hon. gentleman who leads this House, and say for this reason I must have this law applied to Northern Ontario. Now we know where the hon. gentleman stands as a public man. We know why my hon. friend has now a frenzied desire for a new list in the north. He did not always have that desire. He was well satisfied with the list we had in 1904, and I leave it to the judgment of the right hon. gentleman who leads this House whether upon such a picayune, paltry, prejudiced complaint, absolutely without real foundation, when ventilated and analysed,

my right hon. friend can find any ju tifica-tion for departing from these principles which he proclaimed so loudly and so boldly in years gone by, and take away from the province of Ontario, or the sir all st portion of the province of Ontario, the right it has to make its voters' lists for its own people. Now the situation stands as it was. Lists were compiled under the law of the province of Ontario in the northern constituencies, and there is no complaint against them except the complaint of my hon. friend from Rainy River. Is my right hon. friend not satisfied that they were reasonably good lists ? Did he take pains to ascertain whether in previous elections there were any mistakes or inadvertences in the making up of the lists in settled communities in any part of Ontario? If he did not. why should he listen now to my hon. friend's groanings about something which has taken place on lists, which something has now been cured and which lists have been finally revised? How have the lists been made up? Was there anything irregular about making them up? My hon. friend from Rainy River says there was, and the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) says that the hon. member for Rainy River says there was, and therefore it must be true. What was. it? That an enumerator was appointed who happened to be in ti e office of a gentleman who to my know'edge had no thought whatever of becoming a candidate at the time this man was appointed. A government inquiry shows that at the time that enumerator was appointed a proclamation was issued and was posted. I offer that in contradiction to what my hon. friend says.
I contradict it now. I say no proclamation was issued. I inquired from the clerk of the peace and from the judge of the district and I found that no proclamation was issued.

My hon. friend said that no proclamation was posted in these outlying districts because he did not sea it; that is what it amounts to. Whatever charges of irregularities there were, were confined to one polling subdivision, and they were investigated and found to be unfounded. The list for that one subdivision had to be left open or the election postponed. With regard to the appointment of this enumerator, if it was unfair to appoint him why did not the people object? They did not object to his appointment; they approved of it. The Liberal Association of Port Arthur approved of it. They met and considered the situation and nominated from themselves two stalwarts of che party to go around with this man, to watch him, to check his work, to watch the interests of their party and to attend to all matters connected with the making up of the lists. My hon. friend knows that, but he did not mention that as a detail. If
that was so, surely my hon. friend has no reasonable cause to complain or to expect the right hon. gentleman to put him in a position to overcome the majority of something like 2,000 against him in his own riding, as shown by the provincial election. That is the whole grievance.
I deny it emphatically. The hon. gentleman has quoted a number of things which he claims I said at Port Arthur, not one of which is true.

The hon. gentleman's own staunchest supporters in Port Arthur will endorse my statement. He himself knows that this matter was before the Liberal Association at Port Arthur. These men were engaged, they did go around with the enumerator and check his work and report to the Liberal Association at Port Arthur, Surely when the enumeration was done by the government's appointee, and when into every polling subdivision watchful experienced men appointed by my hon. friend's party went with him to check his work, the hon. gentleman can have no complaint. Or if he has any, it can only be against his own partisans. What, however, the hon. gentleman wants is a grievance against the Ontario government, something which will justify him in his appeal to the right hon. the First Minister to provide a means by which he can bolster up his own situation. The hon. gentleman has posed in that district for many years as the great political head. He is in all things, municipal, legislative and federal-he is a sort of poo-bah or panjandrum up there. He dabbles in municipal politics, in local politics and Dominion politics. Here is a case in which, after endeavouring to pull the wires in the legislative avenue, he finds that by some mistake he pulled the wrong wires, and he views the cataclysm of the 8th June in liis riding with so much alarm that he conjures up this imaginary grievance and implores the First Minister to provide a remedy.
He says that the lists were not made up honestly. That is an easy statement to make, but there is not one word of truth in it. Not alone was the enumerator watched, not only was he upon his oath, but I know him to be a gentleman of honour aud rectitude who would not stoop to such a low level as to violate his oath of office.
As regards the cutting down of the appeal to fifteen days in the unorganized districts, the lament of the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) on that point was very pathetitc. In a paroxysm of grief, he said it was preposterous and absurd. Well, who proposed it? No less a personage then the Hon. A. G. Mackay, leader of the opposition in the local House at Toronto. Fer-haps my hon. friend was one of those who so strongly felt that some of the propositions of that hon. gentleman were preposterous and absurd, that he voted against him on the 8th June. But he must bear in.

mind tliat when Mr. Maekay, in Toronto, came to view the situation in the north, he saw that it would be necessary, in order to hold the general elections there on the same day as elsewhere, to shorten the time of appeal.
I have heard the Hon. A. G. Maekay strongly deny that he ever made any such suggestion.
I have heard the hon. gentleman himself deny many things.

If Mr. Maekay did make such a suggestion, he was simply choosing of two evils the lesser. He preferred to reduce the time rather than have the elections in the northern part of Ontario subsequent to the elections elsewhere. But I do not know that Mr. Whitney was obliged to accept that suggestion. Would the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Boyce) let me put him a question? I ask him what he thinks of the reduction of the time for appeal from thirty to fifteen days in the unorganized districts while in the organized it remains at thirty?
I have given my opinion in many respects.
But as to this.

I would be obliged to the hon. gentleman if he would allow me to proceed without Interruption and let me explain in my own way. I propose to give my own reasons though not at the exact moment he indicates.
I am afraid you will forget.

I am not one of those who forget. The hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) cited the posting at Silver Mountain, and no doubt all these instances have been submitted to the First Minister as reasons why these lists should not be used. My hon. friend said that the posting for Silver Mountain poll took place at Port Arthur, but when asked if it also took place at Silver Mountain, he said hq.did not know.
What I said was that the enumerator posted the list in his own office in another riding altogether.
Exactly what I say. But the hon. gentleman does not know that the list was not posted in the place provided by the law and where I have no doubt it was posted.
My hon. friend does not know that it was. My information is it was not, but I do not know from personal knowledge.

No doubt the statement of the hon. gentleman to the Prime Minister was that the list for Silver Mountain was posted in another constituency, and he has - Mr. BOYCE.
not a word on which to ground such a statement. He complains about partisan enumerators. But these enumerators are appointed under the statute, and there wavs no objection against them until now. He complains that the time was cut down to fifteen days. The time before was thirty days for enumeration and thirty for an appeal, but this included fifteen days notice of the time during which the court was to sit. This thirty days is reduced to fifteen and thirty cuts down the time of appeal by five days although I did say the time for appealing and making up the lists in these unorganized districts was altogether too short. At the same time the preparation of the lists in eleven ridings has demonstrated that the work was done regularly, methodically and completely within the respective periods and that it was from an inadvertence over which the government had no control and not from want of time that the irregularities complained of arose. Possibly thirty days, as under the old law, was preferable and it may be that Mr. Whitney regrets that he was so generous as to give way to the suggestion of the leader of the opposition in the legislature. He had either to give way to that or be held up before the people as desirous of doing something unfair and holding elections in the north at a time subsequent to the general elections, thereby getting an advantage in eleven constituencies.
I did not understand how the hon. member made out that the time was only cut down five days.
If my hon. friend will excuse me ; he can read it in ' Hansard ' and figure it out for himself, and then speak in committee.
I think you are wrong, that is all.

We have in those constituencies eleven valid lists duly prepared, under the Ontario law as it stands to-day and duly certified by the judges. Does the right hou. gentleman believe in following the provincial lists where they can be followed ? If he does he has an opportunity to follow the principle which he has announced. If he desires to avail himself of the petty excuses offered by the hon. member for Port Arthur, which when analysed are reduced to nothing but the desire of my hon. friend to save his seat by adding the names of voters who come in at the last moment, in the face of the deluge of the 8th of June in his riding, if the right hon. gentleman is swayed by expediency rather than by principle, he will adopt (he suggestions of my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) ; but if he looks into the question himself, if he will take the word of the government of Ontario or the certificate of the judges as to the existence and regularity of these lists, he will be prepared

to adhere to the principle of provincial lists which he has so long advocated.
The hon. member for Grey (Mr. Miller) has said that the making up of the lists may be postponed by proclamation. Supposing they are, supposing that for any one or two or three years the Ontario government does not make up lists, what better machinery has my right hon. friend for making up the lists than we have at present, provided he will see to it that the law is administered honestly and with due regard to the abuses of the past and the cautions and words of warning administered to him by two of his friends. He has a remedy now, the lists are ready and complete. If an election should be held when the lists are more than a year old, the hon. gentleman has simply to operate under his statute, to see that the law is honestly administered, that the lists are up to date and properly prepared.

I had no.t intended troubling the House at this stage of the Bill with any further remarks, but I desire to answer some of the observations made by the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) during the course of his remarks this morning. He quoted from certain statements of my own at an earlier stage of this debate with a view of showing that in his opinion I was mistaken in saying that the voters' lists in Ontario, having a municipal origin, are not as correct as those made under a system of registration. I think he differed from that. He contended that the Ontario lists owing to their municipal origin, were absolutely correct or as correct as it could be expected lists could be made. I do not wish to spend any time discussing that point because it is a matter of opinion. As the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) has stated this, I wish to meet it with a concrete case, the proofs of which I have under my hand at this moment. In my own county we have ten municipalities. I have examined the corrected voters' lists relating to the revision of the lists in that riding last fall, and I find that the names struck off and added to that list amounted to no less than 759; 533 were added and 226 struck off. This total is largely over 10 per cent of the voting force of that county. To show that it was no sporadic affection but that it was general throughout the county I shall spend a moment giving the figures, which were as

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Were these names added and stricken off on appeal before judges ?

By the judges on appeal.
I think the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) is perfectly aware, as every gentleman from Ontario must be, that in the vastly greater proportion of instances municipal elections in Ontario are conducted upon party lines, and that one of the first nets of the newly elected municipal corporation is to appoint an assessor. That assessor makes his assessment under the statute, and places the names of those whom he assesses upon the assessment roll. That roll is then on a certain day returned to the municipal clerk. That municipal clerk cannot go outside the four corners of that assessment roll in making up his voters' lists, he can only put on those names which he finds on the assessment roll. As the law is now, part of the duty of the assessor is to put on the lists the manhood suffrage voters in the municipality. But we all know as a matter of fact that the assessors do not do so, and that three-fourths of the work done upon the revision of the lists before the county judges, consists in putting on and taking off, or rather changing the position in the municipality of, the hired men throughout the country under the manhood suffrage vote. I give that as a concrete instance of the failure of the municipally compiled lists to obtain the accuracy which the hon. gentleman thinks they have attained.

Will the hon. gentleman
allow me ?

Let me complete my argument. I say as a matter of opinion, based upon some years of actual work, that the municipally made lists, so far as they are municipally made under the Ontario law, are as faulty as lists made by any other method that I know of. The lists made by registration in Manitoba are the best and most accurately made lists we have in Canada.
